name: Napa Valley
description: California's benchmark Cabernet: cassis, cedar and polished tannin from a valley thirty miles long that changed how the world priced New World wine.
funFact: At the 1976 Judgement of Paris a Napa Cabernet beat first-growth Bordeaux in a blind tasting judged entirely by French experts, and the French press spent years insisting it did not count.

serve.how: Decant a young bottle for an hour — Napa Cabernet is built with tannin that needs air before the cassis and cedar separate from the oak. Serve slightly below room temperature in a large-bowled glass. With age the graphite and tobacco notes come forward and the oak recedes, so an older bottle needs less decanting, not more.

composition.summary: Cabernet Sauvignon from a warm, well-drained valley, aged in new French oak.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Cabernet Sauvignon, often with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Napa Valley floor and its benchland, with mountain sub-appellations above.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fully destemmed, long maceration for colour and tannin extraction.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 18–24 months in French oak, a significant proportion new.

composition.process: Warm-climate ripening gives high sugar and full phenolics, extracted through a long maceration and softened by extended barrel ageing.

name: Sonoma Coast
description: Chardonnay grown where the fog rolls in: tighter, saltier and more mineral than the Napa style, with the oak dialled back.
funFact: The Sonoma Coast appellation reaches close enough to the Pacific that fog caps ripening daily, which is why its Chardonnay keeps acidity that inland California loses.

serve.how: Serve chilled but not cold — under about 48°F the saline and mineral notes flatten into simple citrus. Use a standard white glass rather than a large bowl. If the wine seems tight on opening, give it twenty minutes in the glass; coastal Chardonnay often needs a little air to move from lemon to something rounder.

composition.summary: Cool-climate coastal Chardonnay with restrained oak and firm natural acidity.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The fog-influenced western reaches of Sonoma County, close to the Pacific.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Whole-cluster pressed, barrel-fermented, often with partial malolactic conversion.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 9–16 months in French oak, usually with a low proportion of new barrels.

composition.process: Cool coastal ripening preserves acidity, and barrel fermentation with lees stirring builds texture without heavy oak flavour.

name: Willamette Valley
description: America's answer to Burgundy, and the closest it gets: red cherry, forest floor and fine-boned acidity from a cool, rainy valley south of Portland.
funFact: Burgundy's Domaine Drouhin bought land here in 1987 — an unusually direct endorsement, since the family had spent centuries insisting Pinot Noir belonged only in Burgundy.

serve.how: Serve cooler than most reds, around cellar temperature — warm Pinot Noir loses its lift and tastes flabby. Use a wide Burgundy bowl to gather the aromatics, which are the point of the grape. Decanting is rarely needed; if anything, pour and wait rather than aerate aggressively.

composition.summary: Cool-climate Pinot Noir from Oregon's marine-influenced valley floor and hillsides.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Noir.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Willamette Valley and its hillside sub-appellations, on volcanic and sedimentary soils.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Partial whole-cluster fermentation, gentle extraction to avoid hard tannin.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 10–18 months in French oak, mostly used barrels.

composition.process: Cool ripening and gentle extraction preserve aromatics and acidity, with restrained oak keeping the fruit and earth in front.

name: Columbia Valley
description: High desert Syrah and Cabernet grown on irrigated basalt: dark, savoury and structured, with a smoked-meat edge California rarely finds.
funFact: Eastern Washington is a desert — under ten inches of rain a year — so almost every vine is irrigated, giving growers unusually precise control over ripening.

serve.how: Decant young bottles for half an hour to let the savoury and peppery notes emerge from behind the fruit. Serve slightly cool in a large glass. The savoury character builds with a few years in bottle, so a five-year-old bottle usually shows better balance than a one-year-old one.

composition.summary: Desert-grown Syrah and Bordeaux varieties on basalt soils under irrigation.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The vast Columbia Valley of eastern Washington and its sub-appellations.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Destemmed or partially whole-cluster, fermented warm for structure.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–20 months in French and American oak.

composition.process: Wide day-night temperature swings hold acidity while the desert heat ripens tannin, producing dark, savoury and firmly structured wines.

name: Finger Lakes
description: Riesling from glacial lakes in upstate New York — bracing, lime-driven and often off-dry, with the lakes themselves keeping the vines alive through winter.
funFact: The lakes are deep enough not to freeze, and the stored heat they release keeps vineyards on their slopes from being killed by winters that would destroy vines a mile inland.

serve.how: Serve well chilled but let it warm slightly in the glass; a cold Finger Lakes Riesling shows only acid, and the lime and honeysuckle arrive a few degrees later. Check whether the bottle is dry or off-dry before pairing, since both styles are common and the sweetness changes the food match entirely.

composition.summary: Cool-climate Riesling grown on glacial slopes moderated by deep lakes.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Riesling, with some Cabernet Franc and Grüner Veltliner alongside.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The steep slopes above Seneca, Cayuga and Keuka lakes in upstate New York.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool, slow stainless-steel fermentation, often stopped to leave residual sugar.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Little or no oak; brief lees contact in tank.

composition.process: Slow cool fermentation in stainless preserves the aromatic lime and floral character, with fermentation sometimes arrested to balance high acidity with residual sugar.

name: Paso Robles
description: Big, sun-driven Rhône blends and Zinfandel from a region with a fifty-degree daily temperature swing — generous fruit held up by surprising freshness.
funFact: Paso Robles has one of the widest diurnal temperature ranges of any wine region in California, sometimes swinging fifty degrees Fahrenheit in a day, which is what keeps its high-alcohol reds from tasting flat.

serve.how: Serve a couple of degrees below room temperature — at 68°F and above the alcohol dominates everything. A large glass helps the alcohol blow off. Decant young bottles briefly; these are generous, forward wines that show well early and do not demand long ageing.

composition.summary: Warm-climate Rhône varieties and Zinfandel with a wide diurnal swing preserving acidity.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Zinfandel.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The inland hills of San Luis Obispo County, well east of the Pacific.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Warm fermentation with generous extraction.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French and American oak.

composition.process: Hot days ripen fruit fully while cold nights retain acidity, and warm fermentation extracts the plush tannin the style is known for.

name: Sta. Rita Hills
description: A narrow corridor of transverse valleys funnelling Pacific fog inland, producing Pinot Noir with cranberry sharpness and a distinctly savoury edge.
funFact: The Santa Ynez Valley runs east-west rather than north-south — one of very few transverse ranges in North America — which channels cold ocean air directly into the vineyards.

serve.how: Serve cool in a wide bowl. This is a leaner, more savoury Pinot than Oregon or Sonoma gives, so resist warming it to bring out sweetness that was never there. Give it fifteen minutes open; the sage and blood-orange notes need a little air but the wine tires if decanted hard.

composition.summary: Fog-cooled Pinot Noir from an unusual east-west valley on marine sediment.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Noir, with some Chardonnay and Syrah.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Sta. Rita Hills of Santa Barbara County, open to Pacific fog.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Whole-cluster inclusion common, with cool, slow fermentation.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 10–16 months in French oak, largely used.

composition.process: Persistent marine fog extends the growing season, and whole-cluster fermentation adds the savoury, spiced character that distinguishes the appellation.

name: Niagara Peninsula
description: The world's largest icewine region: grapes left to freeze solid on the vine into January, then pressed while frozen for a few drops of concentrated nectar.
funFact: Canadian law requires the grapes to be naturally frozen on the vine at −8°C or colder before picking, and the harvest often happens at night in January because the temperature has to hold through the pressing.

serve.how: Pour small — two ounces is a full serving of something this concentrated — and serve well chilled so the acidity stays sharp against the sugar. Let it warm a couple of degrees in the glass and the lychee and apricot open up. It keeps for days after opening, unlike most wines, because the sugar preserves it.

composition.summary: Icewine pressed from grapes frozen naturally on the vine in midwinter.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Vidal Blanc and Riesling, sometimes Cabernet Franc.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Niagara Peninsula between Lake Ontario and the escarpment.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Grapes pressed while frozen so water stays behind as ice and only concentrated juice runs.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Fermented slowly and bottled young to preserve freshness; oak is rare.

composition.process: Frozen grapes are pressed at sub-zero temperatures, giving tiny yields of intensely sugary juice that ferments slowly to a low alcohol and high residual sugar.

name: Okanagan Valley
description: A desert valley in British Columbia at the same latitude as Champagne, with long summer days producing aromatic whites of unusual intensity.
funFact: The Okanagan sits far enough north that midsummer days run over sixteen hours, which compensates for the short season and gives the aromatics time to build.

serve.how: Serve chilled in a standard white glass. These are aromatic wines, so avoid over-chilling, which locks the florals away. The valley makes everything from bone-dry Riesling to fuller Pinot Gris, so check the style before pairing — the range under one appellation name is unusually wide.

composition.summary: Aromatic northern whites from a semi-desert valley with very long summer days.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Chardonnay.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Okanagan Valley of interior British Columbia, a semi-arid rain-shadow region.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless fermentation to protect aromatics.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly unoaked, with brief lees ageing.

composition.process: Long northern daylight builds aromatic compounds while cool nights hold acidity, and stainless fermentation keeps both intact.

name: Valle de Guadalupe
description: Mexico's wine country, an hour from the US border: Mediterranean heat, saline coastal air and blends that follow no appellation rulebook at all.
funFact: Baja producers blend freely across Bordeaux, Rhône and Spanish varieties in the same bottle, because Mexico has no appellation law dictating what may go together — a freedom European producers do not have.

serve.how: Serve slightly cool in a large glass. Expect a savoury, sometimes saline character from the coastal influence that sets these apart from Californian wines an hour north. Decant young bottles briefly; the herbal and leather notes emerge with air, and many of these wines are made in tiny quantities with little filtration.

composition.summary: Warm-climate blended reds grown near the Pacific under a saline maritime influence.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Nebbiolo, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache and Syrah, freely blended.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Valle de Guadalupe in Baja California, some fifteen miles inland from the Pacific.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Warm fermentation, often with minimal intervention and native yeast.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–24 months in a mix of French and American oak.

composition.process: Mediterranean heat tempered by cool Pacific air ripens the fruit fully while the saline maritime influence gives the finished wines a savoury edge.
